I've cried a few times. I'm in adult health, I couldn't handle pediatric death. It's hard enough watching new widows/widowers. 

Was on-call for my ICU one night, and they called me in to help out as they had a very acute floor and needed extra hands (beyond what the staffing protocol said. Didnt always work out this way). We had a 38 yo female in severe pulmonary distress due to massive PEs. I just remember that she was fully awake, intubated, too unstable to sedate, and being bagged, yet we couldn't get her sats above 75%. The team and this gal fought death for 4, maybe 5 hours, until she could fight no more. One of our residents was openly in tears in the hall by the station. I was sad, frustrated but together until I noticed a coworker of mine sitting at one of our computers watching YouTube with a little boy, looked to be about 8, on her lap. At first I wondered why her kid would be in the hospital at 2 in the morning. Then I remembered she had no sons, just daughters. And it clunked in that the kid was the son of this lady I'd just done postmortem cleaning on. So I had to bolt for the mens locker room to sob for a while. 

I lasted 18 months in the ICU. Until moral injury and burnout got too much, and I went back to step-down, where I'd worked for years prior. 

Now, when I've got a crashing patient, I'm happy to go all out in that emergency. And then ship them off to ICU where they can become someone elses problem.

(Induced coma/sedated) If the sedation is turned down, yes. Or if a toxin (best example is alcohol) is cleared down enough. [I use alcohol as severe alcohol poisoning can inhibit breathing, which would necessitate a ventilator, but also has a fairly short half-life, and cannot be quickly reversed. Heroin/narcotics and benzodiazepines (such as valium or xanax) can be quickly reversed with drugs like narcan, preventing prolonged respiratory depression. 

When I trial a patient to see if they are ready to come off a ventilator, I stop the sedation, which allows them to wake back up. They cannot speak, there is a finger-thick tube down their mouth, past their gag reflex, and their hands are tied down (to prevent them from pulling that tube out.) It is terrifying for them. They dont remember getting the tube put in, and now theres all that plus alarms, smells, and strangers all around. I do what I can to be reassuring, talk them through what is happening, and keep them calm. 

As far as people in comas for months waking up, persistent vegetative states, etc... it's a common trope in soap operas and the like, but to my experience, it really doesnt happen. The brain NEEDS oxygen and glucose. Deprived of those two things, it goes bad real fast. Neurons starved break down, and once broken, they dont restore. Those top layers of the onion rot fast, and rot within minutes of oxygen deprivation. (Hence why CPR is so critical for a person in respiratory or cardiac arrest. Circulate oxygen. Prevent the brain from rotting.) Those layers do not un-rot, allowing the person to wake up. Sometimes toxins or drugs can take a little longer than normal to clear, blood work will give us indications. But that is a day or two, not weeks, and not years.
